title: The Early Years, 0 to 7
reflection: What is one thing my child is likely to copy from me, and what would I like that to be?

questions.q: What does Lesson 4 mean in saying that a child does not arrive as a blank page?
o: Seeds are already in the soil, and the weather of the home helps decide which come up.
Temperament is settled at birth, so a parent can only watch it and adjust to it as it is.
The child already holds the parents’ own habits, which are simply passed on to the next generation.
The first year of care decides the whole character, so everything that matters is formed early.
questions.e: A child arrives with seeds already in the soil, the saṁskāras held in the chitta, and which of them come up depends on the season. A seed is not yet a plant: the home can call forward one kind of tendency or the other.
questions.c: A child arrives with seeds already in the soil; the weather of the home helps decide which come up

questions.q: A grandmother who took in a baby at six months worries that she has missed the first seeds in the garden. Which view fits Lesson 4?
o: The earliest months matter most, so she should now do a great deal extra to make up for what was missed.
Songs and calm help only before birth, so she can no longer offer them to this child.
The welcome begins whenever the child arrives, and she can sing and talk with the child now.
How the early months went is a verdict on her, and she should keep that in mind as she goes on.
questions.e: How a pregnancy went is never a verdict on a parent, and not every child is carried by the person who raises them. The first voices a child hears are the first seeds, and they can belong to a father, a grandparent, an aunt or a neighbour. The welcome begins whenever the child arrives.
questions.c: The welcome begins whenever the child arrives

questions.q: After bath, teeth and a story, a four-year-old keeps calling out from his bed. Which approach fits Lesson 4?
o: State bedtime once, firmly, and then leave the room, so that he learns it means bedtime.
Answer each call in turn until the calling stops of its own accord, however long that takes.
Settle him first with a low voice or lullaby, then say: bedtime is bedtime.
Make the evening quieter from now on, and leave the rest for him to manage.
questions.e: There are two questions, and the order matters. First, what in the evening could change? Second, what can you add that helps him tune: a lap, a low voice, a lullaby, a hand on his back. You can still say “Bedtime is bedtime,” but a limit given to a settled mind lands, while the same words to a mind out of tune mostly bounce off.
questions.c: Settle first, then say the limit

questions.q: What does a four-year-old’s calling and shouting at bedtime show, according to Lesson 4?
o: That he has not yet been taught clearly and firmly enough that bedtime means bedtime.
That he is asking for attention and has found a sure way of getting it from his parents.
That he is testing how far his parent will let him go this time, as children do.
That he is a mind still playing the day, out of tune with the quiet of the room.
questions.e: The calling, the shouting and the floor are only the surface. Underneath is what the child’s mind is going through. When what is inside the child and what is around him are out of tune, the disturbance shows as crying, clinging or shouting. A young child cannot yet tune himself, so he tunes to whatever is nearest.
questions.c: A big feeling is the surface of a mind out of tune with its surroundings

questions.q: A seven-year-old has a temper like his father’s, and his father wants to help. Which approach fits Lesson 4?
o: Work on the temper directly every time it shows, until it has gone altogether.
Show him, by example, how his father keeps his own temper in check, step by step.
Notice where he is patient, and give that room with attention, words and time.
Leave the temper alone, since a tendency he arrived with cannot really be changed by a parent.
questions.e: You don’t have to wrestle the temper. Think of a light in a dark room: notice where he is patient, with the cat, a little cousin, a puzzle, and give that more room. The more the patient side is called up, the more it holds the other in check.
questions.c: Water what is good: call up the tendencies that hold the others in check

questions.q: A grandmother lets a six-year-old watch whatever is on while she cooks. Which view fits Lesson 4?
o: A child learns to choose by being given the choice early, so she can safely leave it to him.
She decides what comes in, and when enough is enough.
The child can pick for himself and she can step in if something frightens him.
Screens should be avoided altogether, since a young mind should take in nothing at all from them.
questions.e: A young child takes in everything, quickly, and cannot yet choose what to let in. Someone has to stand at the door. In a house it means you decide what comes in: which programmes, which company, which words at the table, and when enough is enough.
questions.c: Lend your discernment at the door while the child’s own grows

questions.q: “One harsh line that a child copies from a parent’s worst night has set the child’s character.”
questions.e: One is a single splash. Character is the sum of impressions, and the word is “prevail”: what prevails over many ordinary days. A groove can be re-cut by many ordinary days of something different, and the same groove runs the other way when a child copies a parent’s tenderness.
questions.c: Character follows what prevails over many ordinary days, not one night

questions.q: A parent wants to be a good example for a four-year-old who copies everything. Which approach fits Lesson 4?
o: Try to be a good example all day, so that nothing wrong is ever seen by the child at all.
Choose two or three things the child will copy, and make those the best.
Keep her mistakes well out of sight, so that the example is never spoilt in the child’s eyes.
Explain to the child which of her ways to copy and which to leave alone, one by one.
questions.e: Choose two or three things your child is most likely to copy, and make those your best: how you speak when you are tired, how you say sorry, how you say thank you. A few steady things, repeated, make a deep groove. No one can be a good example all day, and the child also sees you repair.
questions.c: Choose a few things worth copying; repair when you fall short

questions.q: “If a parent remembers on a hard evening that the child is a spiritual being, the evening will grow shorter.”
questions.e: It will not make a night shorter, but it can change who you are looking at. Your child is a spiritual being, the same light, clothed in a growing body and mind, and the seeds and the seasons belong to the clothing.
questions.c: Remembering the one who has arrived changes who you are looking at, not how long the night is

questions.q: In Lesson 4, what does a parent have the chance to do for a child, who is a spiritual being clothed in a growing body and mind?
o: Shape the child into the person the parent hopes for, because the child is still young and open.
Protect the child from every difficult tendency it brought, so that none of them ever comes up.
Wait until the child’s mind has grown enough to show what is within before doing much at all.
Help, guide and serve that being so that it grows strong and can flourish.
questions.e: Over the years of parenting a parent has the chance to help that being, to guide and to serve it, so that it grows strong and resilient and can survive, thrive and flourish on the journey of life, and grow into a meaningful, purposeful life.
questions.c: The aim: help, guide and serve so that the child can survive, thrive and flourish
